extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, and patent practitioners evaluating §101 eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent-eligibility under Alice/Mayo (35 U.S.C. §101) across biotechnology, life sciences, and software/technology patents, drawing on Federal Circuit and district court holdings and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea / natural law / natural phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are "directed to" an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon are prima facie ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include claims described as directed to the abstract idea of using a flag to find music in a category, managing access to functions based on policies, using sensors to collect data and transmitting it to a generic computer, or the natural phenomenon that certain genetic/biological markers correlate with disease. Multiple cases (e.g., Location Based Servs., Cleveland Clinic, Ariosa/Sequenom, Genetic Techs., True Health) hold that such claims are ineligible absent additional inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept — routine and conventional steps insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is directed to a natural law or abstract idea, it must include an 'inventive concept'—something more than well-understood, routine, and conventional activity—to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly held that recited amplification/detection steps, use of PCR, taking routine measurements (e.g., forehead temperature), administering known drugs, or applying conventional clinical techniques do not supply an inventive concept. Examples: Ariosa (cffDNA detection steps were routine), Cleveland Clinic (detection and comparison were conventional), Esoterix (routine techniques), temporal artery thermometer (measuring forehead temperature not inventive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting merely the discovery of a correlation or natural law are ineligible unless extended to a patentable application
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a natural correlation or phenomenon (e.g., biomarker-disease correlation) by itself does not make a claim eligible — the claim must 'extend the discovery' to a patentable method or application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Cleveland Clinic, Athena Diagnostics, and others stress that finding a correlation or natural relationship is not enough; claims that simply instruct to observe or compare values and act upon the correlation without more are ineligible. Courts look for whether the invention transforms or applies the discovery in a novel, non-conventional way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturally occurring compositions (genes, primers) are ineligible unless structurally or functionally altered
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to nucleotide sequences, primers, or other naturally occurring biological materials are ineligible when they are indistinguishable from naturally occurring counterparts, unless the material has been altered or modified so it no longer exists in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRCA1/BRCA2 and related decisions hold that primers indistinguishable from natural nucleotide sequences are not patent-eligible; however, the court noted that primers altered by investigator-induced mutations or chemical modifications (so they cannot be isolated directly from naturally occurring DNA) may be patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functionality or specific technical solution can render claims eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to overcome a problem specifically arising in computer networks or that recite a specific technical improvement to the way computers operate are not directed to an abstract idea and can be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enfish (self-referential table improving database function), DDR Holdings (composite web pages solving a computer-network problem), McRO (automating lip synchronization with limited rules), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system) are examples where courts found claims directed to specific technological improvements and therefore eligible. The specification's teaching that the claim provides a technological improvement is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely adding a generic computer does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that add only the generic use of a computer to an abstract idea typically lack an inventive concept and remain ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts repeatedly rejected claims where the only addition to an abstract idea was implementation on a generic computer (e.g., vertigo management claims, certain data-processing claims). Courts look for a specific, non-generic computer-based improvement rather than mere automation of an abstract task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim elements in an 'ordered combination' can supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept may arise from the specific ordered combination of claim elements, even if individual elements are conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McRO and BASCOM illustrate that the combination of features—installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable filtering for each user (BASCOM), or particular limited rules for animation (McRO)—can provide the required inventive concept. Courts evaluate claims as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims addressing a specific, identified technological problem and providing unconventional solutions are favorable to eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that resolve a specifically identified technical problem with an unconventional solution that provides advantages over prior art are more likely to be found eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amdocs (correlating network accounting records), Trading Technologies (structured interface and graphical user functionality resolving a prior-art problem), and other cases emphasize that unconventional solutions to technical problems support eligibility even if the claimed subject matter touches abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that organize human behavior or long-standing practices are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply recite longstanding human practices or methods of organizing human activity are treated as abstract ideas and are likely ineligible absent additional inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McRO described certain claimed content-filtering and organization tasks as akin to long-standing human methods; Data Engine and other decisions treated organizing and parsing data or tracking human activities as abstract when implemented generically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility analysis requires reading claims as a whole and considering the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts emphasize reading claim language in context — as a whole — and considering the specification to determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and whether it supplies an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data Engine, Enfish, and other cases stress the importance of claim-as-a-whole analysis and that the specification may teach how claimed features produce a technological improvement, which can affect the §101 outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility may present underlying factual questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although eligibility is ultimately a question of law, there may be factual disputes (e.g., whether claimed elements were conventional) that preclude resolution on a Rule 12 or summary judgment where those facts are contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data Engine Technologies held that district courts erred by concluding there were no underlying factual questions for the §101 inquiry; remand was necessary where questions of fact existed about whether claims provided an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/evidentiary posture matters — absence of claim construction or expert evidence can doom §101 defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have granted early dismissal where patentees failed to provide proposed claim constructions or expert testimony necessary to show that claim terms or claimed techniques were not routine or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleveland Clinic and other decisions denied arguments that eligibility challenges were premature when the patentee provided no proposed constructions or expert evidence to rebut assertions that steps were routine/conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic/method claims requiring in vitro testing or that improve accuracy/convenience may avoid being characterized as directed to a natural law at early stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claims that include in vitro testing steps or claim improvements that make diagnosis more convenient, less subjective, or more accurate may not be immediately dismissed as directed to a natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roche Molecular Systems (report recommended denying dismissal as to certain method claims because they required in vitro testing and potentially improved existing diagnostic methods) — courts may treat such method claims differently at early procedural stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming a new treatment that uses a natural law is not equivalent to claiming the natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: A new therapeutic use that employs a natural law can be conceptually distinct from claiming the law itself, though that distinction does not automatically confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Athena Diagnostics dictum: 'claiming a new treatment for an ailment, albeit using a natural law, is not claiming the natural law.' Courts still examine whether the treatment claims include an inventive concept beyond the natural law and conventional steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to specific machines or physical configurations can avoid being abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting a particular machine, sensor configuration, or physical arrangement that specify how raw data are processed or used may not be considered abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thales Visionix (inertial tracking system specifying configuration and method of using sensors), certain 'machine' claims denied being abstract because they recited concrete configurations and methods that improved functioning over prior art.
